source.title: Multilingual Safety Signals Are Multi-Layered: Filtering Safety-Degrading Data for Safer LLMs
source.authors: Jia-Kun Li; Guo-Wei Song; Si-Jia Li; Xing-Wei He; Hong-Zheng Chai; Yuan Yuan

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates harmful-response behavior after fine-tuning on benign or safe-labeled data selected in different ways, but uses a multilingual data-filtering method rather than the original fine-tuning intervention. It does not test the token-position or prefill claims.
record.gate_note: The paper's main contribution is a filtering defense. It evaluates harmful responses after fine-tuning with randomly selected versus filtered data, which bears on benign-data safety degradation, but does not compare the fine-tuned models with an unfine-tuned safety baseline. Its layer perturbation and SAE analyses bear on layer-level safety signals, not per-token KL or localization in a small set of weights or ranks. Results for the paper's own method versus other filtering methods are not treated as direct evidence for the untested claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper takes benign-data safety degradation from prior work (Qi et al., He et al.) as a premise and builds a filter against it. Its safety results compare its own filter, MMSAFE, with Random and other filters (Table 2, H/R relative to Random). It never measures harmful compliance of the unfine-tuned models, so it cannot show that benign fine-tuning raises compliance. The top-20% vs bottom-20% comparison (Fig. 7) also lacks an untuned baseline, and its numbers appear only in a figure. The layer-perturbation and SAE analyses are layer-level filter design, not tests of weight or rank localization (V5) or per-token KL (V3).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that safety-sensitive layers are only partly shared across languages and that safety signals span complementary layers. They report that MMSAFE cuts the average harmful-response ratio by about 60.7% vs random filtering, and beats single-layer LARF by 6.0 points on average (better on 3 of 4 models), with minimal utility loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study filters multilingual fine-tuning data using layer perturbation and safe–unsafe representation scores, then fine-tunes on the selected bottom 20%. It does not use the few-shot harmful or benign fine-tuning tests, per-token KL measurement, or compliant-opening interventions in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The preferred language-specific layer weight varies across models and datasets; the paper reports that λ = 1.0 is a stable default but not always optimal. The preferred number of language-specific layers also varies, with k = 2 best on two of three tested models and best on average. Layer-sensitivity patterns differ by model and language.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-sensitive layers (measured by refusal-count change under layer scaling) are partly shared across 18 languages and partly language-specific; Qwen3 models are more dispersed than LLaMA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multilingual refusal sensitivity is not concentrated in one shared layer across languages and model families.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features at layers 3, 7, 11 and 15 of LLaMA3.1-8B correspond to different harmful concept types.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different layers encode semantically complementary safety-related features.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on the top-20% risk-ranked benign Aya samples yields substantially more unsafe LinguaSafe responses than the bottom 20%, across four models (Fig. 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign-looking data with safety-sensitive lexical or scenario cues degrades safety more than other benign data (relative comparison, no untuned baseline).

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The safety results after fine-tuning are not compared with an unfine-tuned safety baseline, so the absolute effect of benign fine-tuning is unresolved. The paper notes possible language-dependent bias in sensitive-layer discovery and reference prototypes, and possible bias in automatic or translation-based evaluation. It also notes that adaptive or filtering-aware attacks may circumvent the method. No uncertainty intervals or statistical tests are reported for the main safety results.
record.rows_left_out: The per-benchmark and per-dataset harmful-response results in Table 2 and the ablation and sensitivity plots in Figures 4–7 were not separately extracted; the V2 rows use the paper's explicitly reported six-setting average H/R for each model. Utility results were excluded because they do not measure the claim's safety behavior.

untested.parts: No harmful-response rate for the unfine-tuned models, so it never tests whether benign fine-tuning raises compliance. Fig. 7 (top-20% vs bottom-20% Aya) shows that data selection matters but has no pre-fine-tuning baseline.
No per-token KL. The paper only assumes refusal intent shows in the initial tokens, and uses 32 max tokens for refusal detection.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. MultiJail is used only as an evaluation set, after fine-tuning.
Only whole-layer submodule scaling; no weight- or rank-level localization.

missing.what: Top-20% vs bottom-20% ranked Aya fine-tuning unsafe counts on LinguaSafe, four models. This is a relative benign-data selection effect, with values only in the figure and no untuned baseline.
missing.versions: none (V2-adjacent; would bear on V2 only with an untuned baseline)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 limits_scope label is withdrawn. Rows R1–R4 measure the paper's own filter against baselines, which is method performance, not occurrence of the claimed behaviour. Table 6 unsafe counts (evaluator robustness) also have no pre-fine-tuning baseline. Neither paper is an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or sweep over a few to a few hundred harmful examples.

No comparison of harmful-response rates against the same model before fine-tuning, so the study does not establish whether ordinary benign fine-tuning raises compliance relative to the untuned model. It tests data-selection differences after fine-tuning, not the full range of ordinary or carefully chosen benign data.
No per-token KL measurement or analysis of aligned-versus-base output distributions across response positions.
No compliant-start prefilling, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test.
The paper analyzes layers, not whether a small set of individual weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
No test of whether the training data or objective causes safety to be shallow.
No training intervention designed to spread safety beyond the first response tokens, or test of whether such deepening holds up.

rows.subject: LLaMA3-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: LoRA fine-tuning on bottom-20% samples selected by MMSAFE; compared with random selection.

conditions.value: Aya Dataset and Nemotron-SG; average across six benchmark–dataset combinations

rows.measure: Average harmful-response ratio relative to Random (H/R)
rows.note: The paper reports this as the average across six benchmark–dataset combinations. It shows a difference between data-selection methods, not an increase relative to the unfine-tuned model.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with Random (H/R 37.8% vs 100%), i.e. filter performance, not a rate of benign-fine-tuning safety erosion. There is no unfine-tuned baseline. It should not be linked to V2.

rows.subject: LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: LoRA fine-tuning on bottom-20% samples selected by MMSAFE; compared with random selection.

conditions.value: Aya Dataset and Nemotron-SG; average across six benchmark–dataset combinations

rows.measure: Average harmful-response ratio relative to Random (H/R)
rows.note: The paper reports this as the average across six benchmark–dataset combinations. It does not provide an unfine-tuned safety baseline.
rows.check: This is method-vs-Random filter performance (31.8%), with no untuned-model baseline. Not V2 evidence.

rows.note: The paper reports this as the average across six benchmark–dataset combinations. It shows filtering-method differences, not the change from the untuned model.

rows.subject: Qwen3-32B
rows.operation_detail: LoRA fine-tuning on bottom-20% samples selected by MMSAFE; compared with random selection.

conditions.value: Aya Dataset and Nemotron-SG; average across six benchmark–dataset combinations

rows.measure: Average harmful-response ratio relative to Random (H/R)
rows.note: The paper reports this as the average across six benchmark–dataset combinations. It does not compare against the unfine-tuned model.

rows.subject: LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Measured safety-response-count changes after scaling each layer's attention and feed-forward submodules upward and downward.
rows.value: Layer 8 is consistently salient across many languages; other peaks are language-specific, including Layers 12–14 for Japanese and Korean and Layers 18–19 and 29 for Dutch.
rows.note: This is a layer-level finding, not a test of a small set of individual weights or ranks.
rows.check: This is a layer-sensitivity analysis used to design the filter. It is layer-level, not a test of a small set of weights or ranks, so it does not bear on V5.

rows.subject: LLaMA3-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-language layer sensitivity using upward and downward layer-submodule scaling.
rows.value: A small number of layers, especially around Layer 9, show consistently high sensitivity across many languages.
rows.note: Reported as a strongly shared layer-sensitivity pattern.
rows.check: Layer-level sensitivity used for filter design, not V5 localization.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-language layer sensitivity using upward and downward layer-submodule scaling.
rows.value: Sensitivity peaks occur across a wider range of middle and later layers, with many high-sensitivity regions more language-dependent.
rows.note: This is a layer-level distribution finding; the paper describes the pattern as more dispersed than in LLaMA3-8B-Instruct.
rows.check: Layer-level sensitivity used for filter design, not V5 localization.

rows.subject: Qwen3-32B
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-language layer sensitivity using upward and downward layer-submodule scaling.
rows.value: Sensitivity peaks are scattered across deeper layers and are more language-dependent, alongside some repeatedly salient layers.
rows.note: This is a layer-level distribution finding, not a parameter- or rank-localization test.
rows.check: Layer-level sensitivity used for filter design, not V5 localization.

rows.subject: LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Examined SAE-interpreted features activated by harmful queries at selected layers.
rows.measure: Semantic categories associated with layer features
rows.value: Layer 3 is associated mainly with lexical or local semantic cues; Layer 7 with concrete harmful scenarios; Layer 11 with harmful intent and deception; and Layer 15 with broader safety-policy violations.
rows.note: The paper presents these as semantically different safety-related features across layers.
rows.check: SAE feature interpretation by layer. It does not bear on any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: MMSAFE-filtered fine-tuning versus random selection across the four evaluated models
reader_labels.reason: Harmful-response ratios differ substantially with data selection (R1–R4), but the study does not establish that benign fine-tuning increases harmful compliance relative to an unfine-tuned model.
